headline: Florida's early vote is R+1.3 by registration on 3.90 million ballots in the Oct 28 file (Republicans up 185,000 in person, Democrats up 133,000 by mail), still better for Democrats than R+6.0 at six days out in 2022; the official same-point comparison across five states implies a national vote of about D-0.8 (±1.2) against 2022, unchanged from the Oct 27 files, and about D+4.7 (±1.5) against 2024, while the polls say D+8.4 and the app's forecast D+6.7. Nevada is D+5.6 against D+1.9 in 2022, Colorado D+7.3 against D+3.4, Iowa's absentee pool D+12.6 against D+21.9 and Pennsylvania's mail D+40.4 against D+50.0. The news comparisons lean Democratic but the closing days are Republican: Jon Ralston has Nevada at D+31,823 (5.7 points) with Clark County's firewall at 49,000 (13 points), North Carolina passed 2 million ballots Wednesday after running 521,000 ahead of 2022 at the same point, Georgia is past 2.1 million, and in Texas, where 5.7 million have voted and Democratic-primary voters led by 115,000 on Sunday, Republican-primary voters have moved ahead among in-person ballots on theoelections' count.

compare_note: Registered-party margin among early ballots, 2026 vs. the same point in 2024. Florida, Nevada, Colorado, Iowa and Pennsylvania are computed from the state files by the update job (Florida 3,896,546 ballots in the Oct 28 file against the state's 2024 figures at six days out; Nevada 533,749 against Ralston's 2024 count; Colorado 1,220,842 through Oct 28; Iowa 122,585 absentees in the Oct 28 report; Pennsylvania 934,657 mail ballots through Oct 28); Maine is Call the Map's reading of the state file (211,791 ballots through Oct 26). Virginia's early voters are 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (Morris, Oct 12); Ohio's early voters were 41% Democratic and 28% Republican by last primary ballot as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024 (News 5 Cleveland, from Secretary of State data). Every state with party registration is more Democratic than at this point in 2024, Florida most of all because 2024's Republicans had moved to in-person early voting; against 2022 the official comparison is narrower and mixed (Florida R+1.3 vs. R+6.0, Nevada D+5.6 vs. D+1.9, Colorado D+7.3 vs. D+3.4, Iowa D+12.6 vs. D+21.9, Pennsylvania D+40.4 vs. D+50.0), and North Carolina's comparison is computed from the State Board's files.

bullets.title: The official comparison with 2022 covers five states and implies a national vote of about D-0.8, unchanged from the Oct 27 files; against 2024 it reads about D+4.7.
bullets.html: By registration, Florida's Oct 28 file counts 3,896,546 ballots at R+1.3 (mail 727,320 Democrats to 594,210 Republicans; in person 788,316 to 972,927), against R+6.0 at six days out in 2022; Nevada's 533,749 ballots are D+5.6 (mail D+36,871, in person R+7,078) against D+1.9 on the same day in 2022; Colorado's 1,220,842 returned ballots are D+7.3 against D+3.4; Iowa's 122,585 absentees are D+12.6 against D+21.9; and Pennsylvania's 934,657 returned mail ballots are D+40.4 against D+50.0. The app's calibrated slopes turn those into +3.9, +3.1, +3.3, -2.1 and -2.1 points of margin and a pooled implied national vote of about D-0.8 (±1.2), against polls at D+8.4 and the app's forecast at D+6.7. Against 2024 the same files read better for Democrats: Florida R+1.3 against R+11.7 (worth about +8.7), Nevada D+5.6 against R+5.2 (+9.1) and Colorado D+7.3 against D+2.0 (+4.4) pool to about D+4.7 (±1.5); Pennsylvania's mail at D+40.4 against D+24.5 is worth about +3.5 (±3.5) and Iowa's D+12.6 against D+1.3 about +2.5 (±3.3). Arizona's county compilation reads R+0.9 on 1,269,928 ballots with no same-point baseline.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Oct 28
UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 28)
Pennsylvania Department of State daily mail-ballot report via the app's official comparison, Oct 28
CBS Miami/News Service of Florida, Nov 2, 2022 (the 2022 Florida baseline)

bullets.title: Nevada: D+31,823 (5.7 points) after Wednesday, with Clark County's firewall at 49,000 (13 points) and Democrats leading Clark's in-person vote where Republicans led it by 17,000 in 2022.
bullets.html: Jon Ralston's 9 p.m. Oct 28 entry: 'Another winning day for the Dems pushed the statewide lead up to D+31,823 (5.7 points)'; the Clark firewall rose 'to 49,000, or 13 percent,' with 6,600 returned Clark ballots and about 1,000 in Washoe still to be accepted; turnout is 565,480, 'more than half of what I expect the turnout to be,' and he now calls the race 'starting to get out of hand for most Republicans in contested races.' His 6:45 a.m. entry (through Tuesday): Democrats 'won the day by 5,300 ballots and now have a nearly 30,000-ballot lead, or just under 6 percent'; Clark has 342,533 ballots (146,648 in person, 195,885 mail), '41,723 more than the 300,810 at the same point in 2022, or 13.9 percent more'; 'Democrats lead in-person ballots by 5,924, where Republicans led by 16,987 in 2022,' the mail is D+39,392 'a bit behind their 41,365 lead in 2022,' and the combined Clark lead is 45,316 'up from 24,378 in 2022'; urban Nevada is D+50,349 (11.6 points) and rural Nevada R+20,636 (31.1 points), with 87% of the vote urban. He still expects turnout near 1.1 million. The state's Oct 28 file reads D+5.6 on 533,749 ballots against D+1.9 at this point in 2022 and R+5.2 in 2024.
sources: UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 28)
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; county and Secretary of State data

bullets.title: North Carolina passed 2 million ballots Wednesday; through Tuesday it was 521,000 ahead of 2022 at the same point, with Democrats 40% of ballots and Republicans 25%.
bullets.html: State Board of Elections data released Wednesday Oct 28, as reported by Queen City News: 1,961,167 ballots through Tuesday Oct 27, 24.85% of eligible voters and '521,067 more' than at this time in the 2022 general election; Democrats 792,033 (40.4%), Republicans 486,519 (24.8%), unaffiliated 677,533 (34.5%); more than 1.89 million cast in person; Wake 245,298, Mecklenburg 205,095. WCTI reported more than 2 million ballots as of 4 p.m. Wednesday. Call the Map's reading of the Oct 27 file: 36% ahead of 2022's same point, a D+15.6 gap against D+7.5. Through Monday (ABC11), Black voters were nearly 22% of ballots against slightly over 19% of registrants and Hispanic voters about 3%. Early voting ends Saturday Oct 31 at 3 p.m. The app's own file carries the official comparison (2,150,024 accepted ballots through Oct 28).
sources: Call the Map (NC State Board of Elections file), Oct 28
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; Call the Map is an independent tracker

bullets.title: Georgia is past 2.1 million votes, with in-person early voting 22% above 2022 over the same number of days and L2's modeled electorate 54% Democratic.
bullets.html: The Secretary of State's figures as of 4:30 p.m. Tuesday Oct 27 (WRDW): 2,000,452 in-person early votes and 97,382 accepted absentee ballots, statewide turnout 28% with seven days remaining; 2022's full 15 days produced 1,640,652 in-person early votes, so in-person voting is 'up 22% over the same number of days,' and 'overall turnout (including absentee) matches where Georgia stood at this point in the 2022 cycle.' ABC News (Oct 28): more than 2.1 million Georgians had voted as of Wednesday morning per UF Election Lab; L2's modeled party puts the early vote at 54% Democratic, 38% Republican; habitual voters (four of the last four federal elections) are 67% of it against 55% of the early vote a week before Election Day 2022; Georgians who voted in none of the last four are 52% modeled Democratic and 12% Republican, against 51% and 27% at the same point in 2022, and those who voted in two of four 56% to 24% against 54% to 35%. Walker County is 36% ahead of 2022 over the same days (WTVC). Georgia has no party registration; early voting ends Oct 30.
sources: ABC News (Prosperini, Baker and Oppenheim; L2 data), Oct 28
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor whose party figures are modeled

bullets.title: Texas: 5.7 million have voted, more than all of 2022's early vote, and the Democratic-primary lead is shrinking: Republican-primary voters now lead among in-person ballots on theoelections' count.
bullets.html: TexPolls (Secretary of State data through Oct 27): 5,664,689 early ballots, 29.7% of 19 million registered voters; 5,437,603 in person against 3,526,753 on the same day in 2022 (20.0% of voters then), 'up 54%,' and already above 2022's entire early vote of 5,497,027. theoelections through Oct 28: 5,715,252 voted (5,470,313 in person, 244,939 by mail); in-person ballots from Republican-primary-only voters 1,757,395 (32.1%) now exceed Democratic-primary-only voters' 1,699,975 (31.1%), with 1,855,335 (33.9%) from voters with no primary history; the mail runs 34.7% Democratic-only to 26.6% Republican-only. Ryan Data & Research (Republican consultant Derek Ryan, via CBS Texas): through Monday, day 8, 5,105,620 had voted, Democratic-primary history 1,735,883 (34%) to Republican-primary 1,662,676 (33%), a stated lead of 99,615 (the counts imply 73,207), down from 115,499 after day 7; Tarrant County 390,729 (29%), 36% Democratic-primary to 30% Republican. Ryan told NBC 5 that Republicans led by 400,000 at the same point in the last midterm and that 2 million reliable Republican primary voters had not yet voted. ABC News (Oct 28): L2's modeled party has Texas 51% Democratic to 45% Republican against a Republican lead of about 8 points in 2022's final early vote. Early voting ends Oct 30.
bullets.aff: TexPolls and theoelections are independent trackers; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant; L2 is a nonpartisan vendor (modeled party)

bullets.title: Florida: R+1.3 in the Oct 28 file, with Republicans up 185,000 in person and Democrats up 133,000 by mail; the daily Republican gain has grown to about 34,000.
bullets.html: The Division of Elections' Oct 28 file (the app's official comparison) has 2,210,864 in-person ballots, 972,927 Republican to 788,316 Democratic (R+184,611), and 1,685,682 mail ballots returned, 727,320 Democratic to 594,210 Republican (D+133,110): 40.2% Republican to 38.9% Democratic on 3,896,546 ballots, from R+1.0 on 3,517,675 in the Oct 27 file and D+6.7 at twenty days out. The Tallahassee Democrat's reading of the state's Oct 28 morning report (3,524,961 ballots, Republicans ahead by 34,655): the Republican gain was about 9,000 on Oct 26, just under 13,000 on Oct 27 and just over 34,000 on Oct 28, with 845,845 requested mail ballots outstanding (338,037 Democratic, 285,028 Republican, 198,532 no party). FOX 13 (UF Election Lab count of Oct 28): Hillsborough 226,598 ballots (Democrats ahead by 16,392), Pinellas 184,597 (D+3,402), Polk 94,469 (Republicans ahead by 132). Call the Map: Miami-Dade 332,842 ballots, D+4.0, 71% of the county's whole 2022 early vote; statewide Democrats are up 13% on the same point in 2022 and Republicans 1%. At six days out in 2022 the state was R+6.0 (interpolated from the state's Nov 1 and Nov 3, 2022 figures), and at the same point in 2024 R+11.7.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Oct 28
CBS Miami/News Service of Florida, Nov 2, 2022
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets and an independent tracker

bullets.title: Turnout without party: Wisconsin's absentee returns are 2% ahead of 2022, Michigan's 4% ahead plus 216,000 in-person votes, Virginia has passed 2022's final total, Pennsylvania's mail is 2% behind.
bullets.html: Wisconsin: the Elections Commission's report a week out has 513,602 absentee ballots returned (251,092 of them in person) against 503,180 at the same point in 2022 (FOX 11, Oct 27); Call the Map's reading has 764,694 ballots including in-person early votes against 545,461 at the same point in 2022, with Milwaukee County at 66% of its whole 2022 early vote, Dane 64% and Waukesha 71% through Oct 26. Michigan: 1,392,170 ballots as of 7 a.m. Oct 27, 18.8% of active voters, 1,176,375 absentee ballots returned (2,154,870 requested) and 215,795 early in-person votes, against 1,126,246 absentee ballots returned and 1,899,273 requested a week before Election Day 2022 (Secretary of State). Virginia: 1,196,409 early ballots through Oct 27 per Call the Map, about three-quarters in person, against 976,558 in all of 2022's early period. Pennsylvania: 931,700 mail ballots returned through Oct 27, 2% below the same point in 2022, Democrats 609,561 (down 10%), Republicans 233,249 (up 20%), unaffiliated 88,890 (up 8%); D+40.4 against D+50.5 (Call the Map). Ohio: 1,292,227 ballots through Oct 27, 60% of them in person (Call the Map), after Secretary of State LaRose said the state 'could be on track to break another record' (NBC4).
bullets.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets and an independent tracker

bullets.title: Nationally, 40.5 million have voted; McDonald says registered Democrats are outvoting Republicans in about two dozen states, and L2's Westcott says the edge looks like 2022's.
bullets.html: UF Election Lab counted 40,532,275 ballots across 49 reporting jurisdictions in the app's Oct 29 file. Michael McDonald (Spectrum News, Oct 28): 'nearly 40 million Americans have already voted,' with 'about 4-5 million early votes cast every day'; turnout will 'beat the 2022 turnout' and the question is whether it beats 2018's; registered Democrats are outpacing registered Republicans in 'roughly two dozen states'; Texas is 1.75 million votes ahead of four years ago. Earlier (TNND, Oct 26): in the states with party registration about 45% Democrats, 30% Republicans and 25% unaffiliated or other; 'Every other state where I've done this analysis, it's pacing ahead' of 2022 except Pennsylvania and Tennessee. Call the Map's Oct 28 tally is 34,244,936 in 46 states, with its six day-aligned states 9% ahead of 2022. Pluribus News (Oct 23): L2's modeled figures 49% Democrats to 34% Republicans, nearly 60% of early voters over 65, and L2's Paul Westcott: 'The best comparison is 2022, and 2022 was not a blue wave.' The shift from mail to in person continues: Georgia's mail is down by half, Florida's in-person vote is 57% of the total and Republican by 185,000, Texas is 96% in person, Wisconsin's in-person absentee ballots are almost half its returns.
bullets.aff: McDonald is a nonpartisan academic; L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor whose party figures are modeled in states without registration; Pluribus, Spectrum and TNND are nonpartisan

calendar_note: Kentucky's early in-person voting runs Oct 29-31; it is the last battleground opening. Closing dates: Maine's in-person absentee voting Oct 29; Georgia, Texas, Nevada and Arizona Oct 30; North Carolina and South Carolina Oct 31 (North Carolina at 3 p.m.); Michigan, Wisconsin and Ohio Nov 1; Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota and Nebraska Nov 2. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire have no early in-person voting; Pennsylvania's mail ballots must reach county offices by 8 p.m. Nov 3.
cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 49 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 23-28) when these comparisons were compiled; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
signals_verdict: The official same-point comparison with 2022 (Florida, Nevada, Colorado, Iowa and Pennsylvania) implies a national vote of about D-0.8 (±1.2), unchanged from the Oct 27 files: Florida is R+1.3 by registration in the Oct 28 file against R+6.0 at six days out in 2022, Nevada D+5.6 against D+1.9, Colorado D+7.3 against D+3.4, Iowa's absentee pool D+12.6 against D+21.9 and Pennsylvania's mail D+40.4 against D+50.0; against 2024, Florida (R+1.3 vs. R+11.7), Nevada (D+5.6 vs. R+5.2) and Colorado (D+7.3 vs. D+2.0) pool to about D+4.7 (±1.5), so the early vote fits a Democratic year without confirming polls at D+8.4. The news comparisons are bluer where the states lack party registration: Ralston has Clark County's in-person vote D+5,924 where Republicans led it by 16,987 at this point in 2022 and the county's Democratic lead at 45,316 ballots against 24,378, North Carolina ran 521,000 ballots ahead of 2022 at the same point and passed 2 million Wednesday with Democrats 40% and Republicans 25% of them, and Texas's in-person vote is up 54% on 2022's same day; but the closing days are running Republican, with Florida's in-person vote R+185,000 and widening about 30,000 a day, Texas's Republican-primary voters moving ahead of Democratic-primary voters among in-person ballots on theoelections' Oct 28 count, and Pennsylvania's mail returns 2% behind 2022. The next tests are Florida's and Nevada's final two days of in-person voting (Nevada's early voting closes Oct 30), the Republican closing surge in Texas and Georgia through Oct 30, North Carolina's last three days through Oct 31 at 3 p.m., and whether Pennsylvania's remaining 385,000 outstanding mail ballots come back.

signals.title: Nevada is D+31,823 (5.7 points) after Wednesday, Clark County's firewall is 49,000 (13 points), and Democrats lead Clark's in-person vote where Republicans led by 17,000 at this point in 2022
signals.value: Jon Ralston, 9 p.m. Oct 28: 'Another winning day for the Dems pushed the statewide lead up to D+31,823 (5.7 points)' with the Clark firewall 'to 49,000, or 13 percent,' 6,600 returned Clark ballots still to be accepted and turnout at 565,480, 'more than half of what I expect the turnout to be.' 6:45 a.m. (through Tuesday): Democrats 'won the day by 5,300 ballots' for 'a nearly 30,000-ballot lead, or just under 6 percent'; Clark 342,533 ballots, '41,723 more than the 300,810 at the same point in 2022, or 13.9 percent more'; 'Democrats lead in-person ballots by 5,924, where Republicans led by 16,987 in 2022,' mail D+39,392 'a bit behind their 41,365 lead in 2022,' combined Clark lead 45,316 'up from 24,378 in 2022'; urban Nevada D+50,349 (11.6 points), rural Nevada R+20,636 (31.1 points).
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice. Republicans won Election Day 2022 by nearly 50,000 ballots and his model has them winning the rurals by about 56,000; roughly 480,000 to 550,000 votes are still to come on his 1.0-1.1 million turnout models. The state's Oct 28 file reads D+5.6 on 533,749 ballots against D+1.9 at this point in 2022 and R+5.2 in 2024 (the app's official panel).
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet (Jon Ralston); county and Secretary of State data

signals.title: North Carolina passed 2 million ballots Wednesday after running 521,000 ahead of 2022 at the same point; Democrats are 40% of them, Republicans 25%
signals.value: State Board of Elections data released Wednesday Oct 28 (Queen City News): 1,961,167 ballots through Tuesday, 24.85% of eligible voters, '521,067 more' than at this time in 2022; Democrats 792,033, Republicans 486,519, unaffiliated 677,533; more than 1.89 million in person; Wake 245,298, Mecklenburg 205,095. WCTI (Oct 28): more than 2 million ballots as of 4 p.m. Wednesday. Call the Map's reading of the Oct 27 file: 36% ahead of 2022's same point, D+15.6 against D+7.5. Through Monday (ABC11), Black voters were nearly 22% of ballots against about 19% of registrants.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice, and much of the Democratic surge is 2022 Election Day voters moving earlier; Republicans outvoted Democrats on Election Day 2022. Early voting ends Oct 31 at 3 p.m. The app's own file carries the official comparison.

signals.aff: Official data via nonpartisan outlets; Call the Map is an independent tracker

signals.title: Georgia is past 2.1 million votes with in-person early voting 22% above 2022 over the same number of days, and L2's modeled electorate is 54% Democratic
signals.value: Secretary of State figures as of 4:30 p.m. Oct 27 (WRDW): 2,000,452 in-person early votes and 97,382 accepted absentee ballots, turnout 28% with seven days left; in-person early voting 'up 22% over the same number of days' in 2022, and overall turnout 'matches where Georgia stood at this point in the 2022 cycle.' ABC News (Oct 28): more than 2.1 million as of Wednesday morning (UF Election Lab); L2's modeled party has the early vote 54% Democratic to 38% Republican; voters who cast all of the last four federal ballots are 67% of it against 55% a week before Election Day 2022, and Georgians who voted in none of the last four are 52% modeled Democratic and 12% Republican against 51% and 27% at the same point in 2022.
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration, so the direction comes from L2's model, whose 2022 comparisons are for subgroups, not the whole electorate; the same-point turnout match means the surge is mostly mail voters moving in person (mail is down by half). The electorate is old. Early voting ends Oct 30.
signals.src: WRDW (Secretary of State data), Oct 28; ABC News (L2 data), Oct 28
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor (modeled party)

signals.title: Texas: 5.7 million have voted, in-person voting is 54% above 2022's same day and already past all of 2022's early vote, and Democratic-primary voters led by 100,000 where Republicans led by 400,000 in 2022
signals.value: TexPolls (Secretary of State data through Oct 27): 5,664,689 early ballots, 29.7% of registered voters; 5,437,603 in person against 3,526,753 on the same day in 2022, 'up 54%,' and already above 2022's full early vote of 5,497,027. Ryan Data & Research via CBS Texas (through Monday Oct 26, day 8): 5,105,620 voted; Democratic-primary history 1,735,883 (34%), Republican-primary history 1,662,676 (33%), a stated Democratic lead of 99,615 (the counts imply 73,207), from 115,499 after day 7; Ryan via NBC 5: Republicans had 'a 400,000-vote advantage' at the same point in the last midterm and 2 million reliable Republican primary voters had not voted. ABC News (Oct 28): L2's modeled party has Texas 51% Democratic to 45% Republican against a Republican lead of about 8 points in 2022's final early vote.
signals.catch: No party registration: 'party' is primary history or L2's model, and 2022's electorate was unusually Republican. The lead has shrunk each day since Sunday and theoelections' Oct 28 count has Republican-primary voters ahead in person (the separate signal). Ryan expects about 10 million votes. Early voting ends Oct 30.
signals.src: TexPolls, Oct 28; CBS Texas (Jack Fink), Oct 27; NBC 5 DFW, Oct 27; ABC News, Oct 28
signals.aff: TexPolls is an independent tracker; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant; L2 is a nonpartisan vendor (modeled party)

signals.title: Texas's Republican closing surge: by theoelections' Oct 28 count, Republican-primary voters lead Democratic-primary voters among in-person ballots, 1,757,395 to 1,699,975
signals.value: theoelections (as of Oct 28): 5,715,252 voted, 5,470,313 in person and 244,939 by mail; in-person ballots from Republican-primary-only voters 1,757,395 (32.1%), Democratic-primary-only 1,699,975 (31.1%), both 157,608, no primary 1,855,335 (33.9%); mail 84,974 Democratic-only (34.7%) to 65,037 Republican-only (26.6%). On Oct 27 the same count had the in-person split 31.9% Democratic-only to 32.3% Republican-only. Ryan's day-8 Democratic lead (99,615 stated) was down from 115,499 after day 7.
signals.catch: Primary history is not vote choice, and about a third of voters have none. Against 2022, when Republican-primary voters led by 400,000 at this point, the electorate is still far more Democratic; the signal is the direction of the final days, as Ryan predicted with 2 million Republican primary voters still out and 20-30% of the vote expected in the last three days.
signals.aff: theoelections is an independent tracker whose affiliation is not stated; Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant

signals.title: Florida's combined early vote is R+1.3 in the Oct 28 file, with Republicans up 185,000 in person and the gap widening by about 30,000 a day
signals.value: Division of Elections file for Oct 28 (the app's official panel): 2,210,864 in-person ballots, 972,927 Republican to 788,316 Democratic (R+184,611); 1,685,682 mail ballots returned, 727,320 Democratic to 594,210 Republican (D+133,110); combined 40.2% Republican to 38.9% Democratic on 3,896,546 ballots, from R+1.0 on Oct 27, R+0.4 on Oct 26 and D+6.7 at twenty days out. The Tallahassee Democrat's reading of the state's Oct 28 morning report: the Republican lead grew by about 9,000 on Oct 26, 13,000 on Oct 27 and 34,000 on Oct 28; 845,845 requested mail ballots were still out (338,037 Democratic, 285,028 Republican). Call the Map: Miami-Dade D+4.0 on 332,842 ballots, 71% of the county's whole 2022 early vote.
signals.catch: The same-point comparison still favors Democrats: R+6.0 at six days out in 2022 and R+11.7 in 2024 (the app's official panel), and 2022's final early vote was R+6.4. Republicans won Florida's in-person vote by far more in both years; the outstanding mail is Democratic-leaning. Registration is not vote choice.
signals.src: Florida Division of Elections daily file via the app's official comparison, Oct 28; Tallahassee Democrat, Oct 29; Call the Map, Oct 28
signals.aff: Official data; Call the Map is an independent tracker

signals.title: Pennsylvania's mail returns trail 2022 by 2%, with Democrats' returns down 10% and Republicans' up 20%
signals.value: Call the Map (state file of Oct 28, ballots through Oct 27): 931,700 mail ballots returned, 39,736 that day, '2% fewer' than the same point in 2022; Democrats 609,561 (65%, down 10%), Republicans 233,249 (25%, up 20%), unaffiliated 88,890 (up 8%); D+40.4 vs. D+50.5 (Nov 1, 2022: 674,987 Democrats, 194,670 Republicans) and D+24.3 at the same point in 2024. Philadelphia 82,801 returned (D+80.7), Allegheny 115,258 (D+56.4), Montgomery 86,344 (D+48.5), Bucks 76,919 (D+29.7). The state's Oct 28 file: 934,657 returned; the app's official panel reads D+40.4 against D+50.0 in 2022 and D+24.5 in 2024.
signals.catch: Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year (D+50 at this point in 2022, when Republicans won the national vote), and Democrats are shifting to Election Day voting; the state has no in-person early voting, so there is no in-person count to offset it. Call the Map notes 2022's file counted every ballot with a return date, including ballots later set aside, so the comparison is not fully like for like. The official comparison is on the app's panel, so this signal is the turnout picture only. About 385,000 approved ballots were still outstanding.
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file

signals.title: Wisconsin's absentee returns have caught up with 2022 (2% ahead a week out), but the last county read had Milwaukee down 10% and Dane down 15%
signals.value: Wisconsin Elections Commission report a week before the election (FOX 11, Oct 27): 513,602 absentee ballots returned, 251,092 of them cast early in person, against 503,180 returned a week before the 2022 election. Call the Map's reading (Oct 27): 764,694 ballots including in-person early votes against 545,461 at the same point in 2022; through Oct 26, Milwaukee County had cast 66% of its whole 2022 early vote, Dane 64% and Waukesha 71%. The last county comparison (Dairyland Sentinel, data through Oct 23) had Milwaukee County down 10.1%, Dane down 14.9% and Madison down 21.3% while Waukesha was up 2.4% and Washington up 22%.
signals.catch: No party registration, so this is turnout only. The statewide gap has closed from 10% behind on Oct 22 to 2% ahead, so the county lag may have closed too; in-person absentee voting runs through Nov 1 and both parties pushed voters away from mail. The county analysis is by Joe Handrick, a former Republican legislator. The part that leans Republican is that the Democratic counties are further behind their 2022 totals than suburban Waukesha.
signals.src: FOX 11 (Wisconsin Elections Commission data), Oct 27; Call the Map, Oct 28; Dairyland Sentinel, Oct 23
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet and an independent tracker; the county analysis is on a conservative-leaning site by a former Republican legislator

signals.title: Michigan's absentee returns are 4% ahead of 2022 a week out, plus 216,000 early in-person votes that did not exist then
signals.value: Secretary of State release, Oct 27 (7 a.m.): 1,392,170 ballots cast, 18.8% of active registered voters; 1,176,375 absentee ballots returned of 2,154,870 requested (2,016,031 from the permanent list) and 215,795 early in-person votes. One week before the 2022 election, 1,899,273 absentee ballots had been requested and 1,126,246 returned. No newer release had been posted by Oct 29.
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction, and the department itself cautions that higher early numbers 'do not necessarily mean' higher overall turnout. About 94% of requests come from the permanent list, which inflates the request count. Early in-person voting runs through Nov 1.

signals.title: Ohio's early electorate flipped from Republican to Democratic by last primary ballot, and LaRose says the state may break its early-vote record
signals.value: Democrats had returned about 94,000 ballots, unaffiliated voters a little more than 67,000 and Republicans nearly 64,000 (by last primary ballot), per the Ohio Capital Journal from Secretary of State data through Oct 12-13; News 5 Cleveland put Democrats at 41% and Republicans at 28% of nearly 230,000 early votes as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024. A week out, 68% of absentee ballots had been returned and Secretary of State LaRose said 'if trendlines continue we could be on track to break another record' (NBC4, Oct 27); Call the Map's count through Oct 27 is 1,292,227 ballots, 60% of them in person.
signals.catch: 2024 was a presidential year, and Ohio Republicans are shifting from mail to later voting: mail requests were 631,079 vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022. 'Party' is the last primary ballot pulled; seniors are more than half of ballots. No newer party breakdown has been published since Oct 15.
signals.src: Ohio Capital Journal (Ohio Secretary of State data), Oct 15; NBC4 Columbus, Oct 27; Call the Map, Oct 28
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlets; official data; Call the Map is an independent tracker

signals.title: Virginia's early vote has passed 2022's final early total, 1.2 million against 977,000
signals.value: Call the Map's count: 1,196,409 early ballots through Oct 27, 76,879 of them that day, about three-quarters in person; VPAP's Oct 26 count was 1,183,919 against 976,558 in all of 2022's early-voting period (DC News Now, Oct 27).
signals.catch: Virginia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction, and the comparison is to 2022's final, not the same point. Virginia's 2025 governor race already showed a Democratic swing, so high turnout here says less about the national picture. The modeled party lean is in the separate L2 measure.
signals.src: Call the Map, Oct 28; DC News Now (VPAP data), Oct 27
signals.aff: Independent tracker; VPAP is a nonpartisan tracker of state data

signals.title: Maine's absentee vote is 38% ahead of 2022 with unaffiliated voters up 60%; the party gap is a point narrower than 2022's
signals.value: 211,791 ballots through Oct 26 (Call the Map's reading of the Secretary of State file, 24,587 that day): Democrats 104,534 (49%, up 32% on 2022), Republicans 45,565 (22%, up 29%), unaffiliated 61,692 (29%, up 60%); a D+27.8 gap vs. D+28.7 at the same point in 2022 (79,262 Democrats, 35,356 Republicans) and D+16.6 at the same point in 2024. In-person absentee ballots are 115,793 (52%) and mail 106,172.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice. Against 2022 the gap is a point narrower, so the Democratic reading comes from turnout and the 2024 comparison, and the unaffiliated voters who decide the Collins race are the fastest-growing group. In-person absentee voting ends Oct 29.
signals.src: Call the Map (Maine Secretary of State absentee file), Oct 28
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated

signals.title: Clark County's mail vote is slightly less Democratic than at this point in 2022, and the statewide in-person vote is Republican
signals.value: Ralston, Oct 28 (through Tuesday): Clark's mail ballots are D+39,392, 'a bit behind their 41,365 lead in 2022,' while the county's in-person vote is D+5,924. The state's Oct 28 file (the app's official panel): in-person ballots statewide 88,477 Republican to 81,399 Democratic (R+7,078) on 218,964, mail 132,145 Democratic to 95,274 Republican (D+36,871) on 314,785. Call the Map's Oct 25 reading had Clark's mail at D+18.3 vs. D+24.1 at the same point in 2022.
signals.catch: Democrats are shifting from mail to in person, which the county-wide figures absorb (Clark overall is D+45,316 against D+24,378 in 2022); mail is about 59% of the vote this year against about half in 2022. Registration is not vote choice.
signals.src: Nevada Independent, Oct 28; UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 28)
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; Secretary of State data

signals.title: L2 and McDonald: Democrats' national early-vote edge looks like 2022's, which was not a blue wave
signals.value: Michael McDonald (Spectrum News, Oct 28): 'nearly 40 million Americans have already voted,' about 4-5 million a day, and registered Democrats are outvoting registered Republicans in 'roughly two dozen states'; earlier (TNND, Oct 26): in the party-registration states about 45% Democrats, 30% Republicans, 25% unaffiliated or other, and every state he has analyzed is pacing ahead of 2022 except Pennsylvania and Tennessee. Pluribus News (Oct 23): L2's modeled figures 49% Democrats to 34% Republicans, nearly 60% of early voters over 65, and L2's Paul Westcott: 'The best comparison is 2022, and 2022 was not a blue wave.' UF Election Lab's Oct 29 count is 40,532,275 ballots; Call the Map's six day-aligned states are 9% ahead of 2022.
signals.catch: L2's party is modeled in states without registration, and the 2022 comparison is Westcott's characterization, not a published same-point table. Democrats' 2022 early-vote edge preceded a national vote they lost by about 3 points, which is why the edge alone says little; the turnout gains are concentrated in states whose Election Day vote was Republican in 2022.
signals.src: Spectrum News, Oct 28; TNND, Oct 26; Pluribus News (Reid Wilson), Oct 23; Call the Map, Oct 28
signals.aff: McDonald is a nonpartisan academic; L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor (modeled party)
